subject: Anthropology
title: Early Tool Use
description: A short lesson to help you apply Early Tool Use.

hook.text: A sharp stone flake cuts through hide faster than teeth. 2.6 million years ago, someone figured that out.

buildup.text: The oldest known stone tools are Oldowan choppers — simple rocks with edges chipped off by striking.

discovery.text: These tools let early hominins access meat and marrow, opening a high-energy food source that fueled brain growth.

twist.text: We're not sure who made the first tools. It may have been Homo habilis — or even late Australopithecus.

climax.text: Tool use marks a turning point: instead of adapting bodies to the environment, hominins adapted the environment.

punchline.text: The first tool changed the rules of survival.

quiz.question: What are Oldowan tools?
options: Simple stone choppers with chipped edges

details.summary: The earliest known stone tools date to about 3.3 million years ago — earlier than the genus Homo. Tool use marks a critical threshold in human evolution, enabling access to new food sources, changing selective pressures on brains and hands, and jumpstarting cumulative cultural evolution.
details.whyItMatters: Tool making was the gateway to cumulative culture — each generation could improve on the previous generation's technology. This ratchet effect distinguishes human cultural evolution from other species and ultimately produced the entire technological.
takeaways: The earliest stone tools date to about 3.3 million years ago
Tool use preceded the genus Homo and drove brain evolution
It enabled cumulative cultural evolution through generational improvement

faq.question: Who made the first stone tools?
faq.answer: The oldest known tools from Lomekwi 3 in Kenya predate the genus Homo, suggesting australopithecines or related hominins made them. This challenges the assumption that only our genus was capable of tool manufacture and pushes the origins of technology deeper into our evolutionary past.

faq.question: Why are stone tools so important for understanding evolution?
faq.answer: Stone tools preserve well and reveal cognitive complexity — the maker had to select raw materials, plan strikes, and understand fracture mechanics. Increasingly sophisticated tools over time document the growth of abstract thinking, planning ability, and cultural transmission in the hominin lineage.
